scripts.long: Take a look at these feet. They aren't human, and they certainly don't belong to a bird. They are powerful lion paws. Now look higher up the back of this figure. That's a bumpy, armored ridge resembling the skin of a crocodile. And the overall posture? It mimics a heavily pregnant mammal standing upright on its hind legs. What kind of ancient creature combines a lion, a crocodile, and a pregnant animal into one tiny, brilliant-blue package? More importantly, what could this bizarre hybrid possibly have been used for? If you think you know, pause and drop your guess in the comments right now! Ready for the reveal? This is a stunning, miniature statuette of the ancient Egyptian goddess Taweret! Crafted during the Ptolemaic Period, between 332 and 30 BCE, this tiny figure stands just eleven centimeters tall. She is made of an incredibly vibrant material called glassy faience, which gives her that luminous, deep-blue sheen. Far from being a monster, this composite beast was actually one of the most beloved and comforting figures in the ancient Nile Valley. So, how was she used? Taweret was the ultimate protector of mothers, pregnant women, and newborn babies. In ancient Egypt, childbirth was incredibly dangerous. To shield vulnerable mothers and infants from malevolent spirits and invisible demons, people turned to magic and protective deities. Taweret's terrifying appearance was entirely intentional. By combining the most fearsome predators of the Nile—the aggressive hippopotamus, the deadly crocodile, and the fierce lion—she possessed the ultimate power to scare away evil. Women would keep statuettes like this in the home, especially in rooms designated for birth, or wear smaller versions as amulets. Her swollen belly represents fertility and the promise of new life, while her menacing features served as a divine bodyguard. This protective role wasn't unique to Taweret. She was often paired with another popular household deity named Bes, a dwarf god with lion-like features who protected homes through music and loud noises. Throughout ancient Egypt, artisans crafted thousands of these protective amulets and figures using faience. Faience wasn't just chosen because it looked beautiful; the glassy, glittering blue-green color itself held deep symbolic meaning. It represented the fertile waters of the Nile, vegetation, and the eternal cycle of rebirth, amplifying the protective magic of the object itself. This particular statuette originates from Egypt during the Ptolemaic Period, a time when Greek rulers—descendants of Alexander the Great's general Ptolemy—governed Egypt but embraced traditional Egyptian gods. This piece represents a high point of late Egyptian faience production, showcasing incredible detail despite its small scale. It eventually made its way out of Egypt and was purchased by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1926, thanks to a generous gift from Edward S. Harkness, a major philanthropist who helped build the Met's world-class Egyptian collection. Today, you can see this beautiful protective goddess in person at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City, housed within their massive Egyptian Art galleries. It remains a powerful testament to the universal human desire to protect our children and find comfort in the face of life's greatest uncertainties. Now, here is a question for you: if you had to design your own protective hybrid animal guardian today, which three animals would you combine to scare away bad vibes? Let us know in the comments!
scripts.shorts: This terrifying hybrid of a pregnant hippo, a lion, and a crocodile was ancient Egypt’s ultimate bodyguard! Meet Taweret, the goddess of childbirth. Crafted over two thousand years ago from brilliant blue glassy faience, she was designed to protect vulnerable mothers and newborns. Childbirth was incredibly risky back then, so Egyptians combined the Nile's deadliest beasts into one protector to literally scare away evil spirits.
